THE NARROWS
Ten o'clock, and the light has almost gone. Davie Lennox and his nephew Tam are hauling creels at the mouth of the Narrows, where the deep water starts.

Tam has been fishing with his uncle for three summers and he knows the sounds of the boat by heart: the winch, the creel on the rail, the gulls. Tonight there are no gulls. "Davie. Where have the birds gone?"
Davie doesn't answer. The rope on the winch has gone tight. Not creel-tight. Tight like something has taken hold of it and is pulling it down, slowly, with all the time in the world. The stern dips.
The yellow marker barrel rolls across the deck. "Cut it," says Davie. "Cut the rope." Tam has the knife in his hand when the water beside the boat goes white.
